Where does Boston Admin stand?

Boston Admin is a city in Massachusetts. Each of its measures is set here against the US average, and beside the places most like it.

How does Boston Admin compare with admins of every size?

Each dot is a US admin of about 25,000 people or more, placed by its population across and by the measure you choose up the side. The colours split the admins into fifths, and the map shows where each one is.

Ask the chart

Of the 36 admins of 500,000 people or more, only six pay more than Boston Admin, San Francisco the most at $180K. Detroit pays the least, at $40K.

In 119 admins, 98 of them in California and most of them under 100,000 people; Los Altos leads at $4.5M. Of the 36 admins of 500,000 or more, only San Jose, at $1.4M, San Francisco, Los Angeles and San Diego.

In Everett, where a home costs 10.3 years of pay; Boston Admin, at 9.2, is seventh of the 53. Newton has the state’s most expensive homes, $1.4M, but its pay is high too, so a home there costs 5.7 years.

Who works here, who lives here, who commutes out

Boston has 719K jobs and 348K working residents. 190K people do both: they live and work in Boston. Commuters fill the other 528K jobs, and 157K residents commute out to work elsewhere.

Who commutes out, and which way more go

348K Bostonians have jobs. 190K work in Boston; 157K, almost half, work somewhere else, mostly west, where the jobs are. Cambridge alone takes 25K, one in six, and is the only one of the five largest partners that takes more than it sends.

Where does Boston Metro stand?

Boston Metro is the labor market around Boston Admin: 5.0 million people across seven counties in Massachusetts and New Hampshire. Its measures are set here against the average US metro, and beside the metros most like it.

How does Boston Metro compare with metros of every size?

Each dot is a US metro, placed by its population across and by the measure you choose up the side. The colours split the metros into fifths, and the map shows each one at its most densely settled point.

Ask the chart

Only four of the 376: San Jose, at $203K, San Francisco, at $164K, Seattle, at $127K, and Naples, Florida, a metro of 416,000 people, at about the same, $115K. New York, four times Boston Metro’s size, pays $104K.

In 16 metros, 13 of them in California or Hawaii; San Jose leads at $1.6M. Among the 54 metros of a million people or more, only five: San Jose, San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego and Seattle.

In 12 of the 54 metros of a million people or more: Los Angeles takes 10.7 years of pay, San Diego 10.0 and New York 6.5, against Boston Metro’s 6.2. Pittsburgh, at 2.8 years, is the easiest.

How does Boston Admin compare with Boston Metro?

Boston Admin is Boston Metro’s largest city, yet only 13 of every 100 people in Boston Metro live there. Homes in Boston Admin cost more than across Boston Metro, pay is a little lower, and unemployment is a little higher.

    Two workforces

    Sorted into rows, the same dots give the two counts. Jobs located here are the grey and teal rows together: 688K. Jobs held by residents are the grey and orange rows: 334K.

    The work that happens in Boston

    The bigger of the two counts first: the jobs inside the boundary, filled by residents and commuters alike. Health care is the largest at 21%, then professional services at 15%, then education and finance.

    Bars are ranked by jobs located here and hold that order for the next two beats, so a sector never moves. Only what is measured about it changes.

    What Boston’s residents do

    The narrow bar is the second count: the jobs residents hold, wherever those jobs are. It sits inside the wide bar almost everywhere, which is the commuter surplus read sector by sector.

    The gaps carry it. Finance and insurance has 3.4 jobs here for every resident who works in the field. Manufacturing and management of companies are the only two where the narrow bar runs past the wide one.

    What the city does more of than its metro

    A mix on its own says little, because most places look like the region around them. The same rows now show each sector’s share of the city against its share of the metro.

    Finance and insurance is 1.9× the metro’s share. Retail, construction, wholesale and manufacturing sit well below parity: the metro does them, the city mostly does not. The hollow marks repeat the reading for residents, and they cluster near 1× — the specialisation belongs to the workplace, not to the people who live here.

    Each sector’s share of the city’s jobs, divided by its share of the metro’s. 1× means the city leans on that sector exactly as much as the metro does; 2× means twice as much.

    The city is part of the metro it is measured against, so a place this large is pulled toward parity. Read the distance from 1×, not the raw figure.

    Extras

    Your City’s Most Specialized Industries

    Of the tradable industries above, these are the ones Boston does an unusual amount of. Each is measured against the national benchmark: a score of 1.0 means the industry takes up the same share of jobs here as it does across the country. Anything higher means the city is more concentrated in it than the country is — and the further past 1.0, the more distinctive it is.

    The same measure, now set against four cities of similar size and economic make-up. The tick on each row is the average of those four — where Boston’s mark runs past it, the city is more specialized in that industry than its peers; where it falls short, less. Hover any row to see the cities behind the average.

    The same measure, now read against every US metro at once — the teal dot is where the Boston metro lands. Hover any mark for the city and figures behind it.

    Take the share of your city’s jobs that sits in an industry, then divide it by the share of jobs that same industry holds nationally. Economists call the result revealed comparative advantage, or RCA.

    If an industry is 4% of jobs in your city and 1% of jobs nationally, the score is 4.0 — four times more concentrated here than in the country at large. A score of 1.0 means exactly average, and below 1.0 means the industry is thinner here than it is elsewhere.

    A high score doesn’t automatically mean a big industry — it means a distinctive one. Employment is carried in the row tooltip, and in the dot form by the size of each dot.

    Switch to Compare with peers above to hold the same scores against four metros in a similar position.

    In this view each peer is scored exactly the same way against the same national benchmark, and the tick on every row is the average of those four. Comparing against the country at large mostly tells you that Boston is a large, wealthy city; comparing against metros in the same position tells you something you can act on.

    Hover any of the four to see how it stacks up against Boston:

    Hovering a row in the chart shows each city individually, so you can see whether the average reflects the whole group or is being pulled by one outlier.

    Glossary

    The terms this tool uses, and how each is measured.

    Complexity

    Complexity measures the knowledge an industry takes to run. Work that needs many people holding many different specialized skills, such as medical devices, financial engineering and research instruments, is complex. Work that almost anywhere can do, such as food service, retail and basic construction, is not.

    It matters because complex work is hard to copy. Places that hold it tend to pay more, to weather downturns better, and to find it easier to move into the next complex thing, because the know-how is already in the room. A metro’s complexity is the mix of its industries weighted by how much of each it does.

    Tradability

    Each industry is placed in a tier by how much of what it makes can be sold to someone outside the metro.

    Traded
    sells most of its output outside the metro, so its earnings are new income arriving here
    Partly traded
    sells some outside and some to the people already here
    Local
    serves the people already here; the customer has to be standing there

    The tiers are cuts on a continuous measure, so an industry near a cut could fall the other way.

    Specialization

    An industry counts as a specialization when the metro does more of it than the country does. The measure divides the industry’s share of jobs here by its share of jobs nationally: 1.0× is exactly the national rate, 2.0× is twice the national share.

    It says nothing about size. A small industry can be a powerful specialization and a large one can be entirely ordinary. This measures what is distinctive about the metro, not what employs the most people.

    Metro area

    A metropolitan statistical area (MSA) is how the US Census draws the functional city: a dense core and every county tied to it by commuting. It is the closest official shape to a labor market, the area within which people can change jobs or homes without changing lives.

    The Boston MSA, Boston-Cambridge-Newton, has 130 places and 5,025,517 people (2024). Boston itself holds 13.4% of them. That is why most of what follows is read at the metro scale.

    Peer metros

    The reference build compares Boston with five peer metros: Washington, Seattle, San Diego, Denver and Baltimore. The figure for each industry is the metro’s share of its jobs measured against the five peers’ share taken together, instead of against the nation’s: 1.0× is the same share as the peers, 4.5× four and a half times theirs.

    The ranking’s black mark is the peers’ own rate against the nation, which follows from the two: where it falls short of the metro’s bar, the metro is the more specialized of the six. The “Against peers” order ranks the industries by that lead, the metro’s rate less the peers’, and draws it as the bar from 0: to the right where the metro is ahead, to the left where it is behind.
